caption: Still purging after months of tretinoin? #creatorsearchinsights #acnepurge #greenscreen
on_screen_hook: It's been over three months and you're still purging. That's not purging.
transcript: It's been over three months and you're still purging. That's not purging. In fact, I'd be willing to bet that for 99.999% of you guys it was never purging in the first place. Purging? It's real. It can happen, but it's not as common as the internet would have you believe. Purging refers to the temporary increase in the number of acne spots that you get when you start a topical that increases the rate of skin cell turnover. Typically that would be a retinoid, but in theory it can happen with other things, but in reality it's rare. Importantly, when it does happen, it does not go beyond three months. An increase in acne or continued acne beyond three months is not purging. It's either skin irritation that's worsening the acne, or your acne is not adequately controlled by topical retinoids.

creator: drarielostad
caption:
Not all aesthetic treatments are created equal—and some come with risks that deserve serious consideration.

In this video, Dr. Ariel Ostad shares a concerning case involving AlloClae performed at another practice. The patient developed a severe reaction at the injection site, leading to redness, inflammation, pain, and ultimately an abscess, requiring medical intervention.

Dr. Ostad also addresses a larger issue: he does not recommend AlloClae, citing both safety and ethical concerns. Because
transcript: Hi everyone. I wanted to spend a few minutes to talk to you about a product called Allocay which is basically taking harvesting fat from a cadaver from unfortunately a dead person and reutilizing it as a fat graft. I don't believe in that. I wanted to tell you my experience with a patient that I saw a few days ago who had basically a fat transferred utilizing this product as a cadaveric, what we call taking it from a dead person, irradiating the product to reduce the risk of infection and reinjecting it. It's commonly used basically as a source of fat to enhance breast for using it for buttock enhancements, using it for deformities whether somebody has let's say irregularities from liposuction or scars and I am a big proponent of using fat but it's about utilizing your own fat which is what we call otologous fat. I understand there are patients who may not have enough body fat to basically do that but in terms of utilizing it from a cadaver I just not only find it unethical but I also feel like it's unsafe. The patient who I saw had a massive reaction with what we call fat necrosis with having what we call oil cyst and a secondary infection. He was in a lot of pain in his buttock. We had to drain the area, we had to put them on antibiotics and it had to be drained a couple of times in order for basically taking all of that fat out. Basically the reaction was that your body can react to that fat because it's not your own fat and then in addition the fat that's basically harvested as much as maybe it's harvested, it's put in a syringe, it's maybe clean, it's irradiated to reduce infection. I'm not sure if it really completely reduces that risk 100% just because there is an issue with rejection where therefore you can get basically fat necrosis. So it's just something that I wanted to bring to your attention, you may hear about it but I just wanted to tell you that I just don't think that that's actually a great treatment.
